title: Long Division Frame
description: Divide place by place from the biggest place down, say what is left at each step, and write a zero only when the number is smaller than the divisor.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

writeup.why: Divide a number place by place from the biggest place down, and find out exactly when a zero belongs in the answer.
writeup.look: A long division frame under place headings, a working window above it naming the place, a multiple strip beside it and a check bar underneath.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Long Division Frame' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the steps finished against the steps this division needs, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each quotient digit settles, zero included, and the second fixed at the number of places being worked. On the last phase it carries the check instead, the rebuilt number against the dividend. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The working window runs across the top of the working area, 640 by 70 at 300,210, holding the number being divided at this step with its place name written after it, fifteen tens and never a bare fifteen. The multiple strip stands at the right, 200 by 510 at 950,210, nine rungs reading the divisor times one to times nine in rose; the largest that fits is dragged to the frame, and a rung bigger than the working number is drawn but will not lift. The frame fills the middle, 640 by 360 at 300,290: place headings from thousands to ones across its top in columns 110 wide, the quotient row directly under the headings, then the bracket with the divisor in amber at its left and the dividend in deep blue under it. Each quotient digit settles above its own place in green; the multiple is written in rose under the working number and taken away, and what is left drops into the left slot, 220 by 64 at 64,300, in vermilion. The bring down arrow beside the next digit stays unlit until the left slot holds a number, and then brings that digit down beside what is left, so the next working number is seen being made. The zero gate is a hinged cover over the quotient cell of the step in hand. It takes a zero only when the working number is smaller than the divisor and writes it in grey at full size; a zero offered at a step that is not smaller is handed back with the rungs of the strip that fit lit, at least the first of them, and the child's offer is written beside the cell. The check bar runs under the frame, 640 by 60 at 300,664, multiplies the divisor by the quotient, adds the remainder and slides the result under the dividend so the two can be matched digit for digit. The blocks bay stands at the lower left, 220 by 340 at 64,384, three small cards for one block's divisions with a total line under them, its label saying that the block's total is the sum of the three quotients. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a quotient digit, a leftover or a check is asked for. The zero key writes a zero into the cell in hand and nowhere else, and it is the key the gate reads. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion; a multiple of the divisor, tried on a ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose; and a zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because what is left over is told by the dish or the slot it sits in, a quotient digit by the row it sits in, and a multiple by the rung or the column that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour, and every rule, bracket, cell edge and guide line is near-black. Grey never means faint: a zero in the quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A quotient digit never stands anywhere but above its own place, and the place headings never scroll or shrink. A zero the gate has taken is exactly the size of every other digit in the row, because it is holding a place, and a thinner zero is the one that gets left out.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last division the child worked, every quotient digit above its place and every leftover still written, with the check bar matched under the dividend.

phases.win: the first quotient digit lands above its place and what is left is carried to the next place
phases.does: divides the digit in the biggest place, writes the quotient digit above it and says what is left
phases.goal: long division starts with the digit in the biggest place, and what is left is carried on
phases.says: Which place is the biggest? Share that one first.
phases.check: Away from the screen: share nine hundreds, three tens and six ones among four envelopes. Say which notes you shared first and what you changed.
phases.feels: the biggest things go round first, and whatever is left is changed down into the next place rather than thrown away
phases.hands: Hand a group eight hundred-rupee notes, four tens and six ones in play money, and three envelopes. Ask them to share the hundreds first. When two hundreds will not go round, change them for twenty tens and carry on with the tens, then the ones. Then ask what would have happened if they had shared the ones first.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which place is the biggest? Second rung, the phase's: how many of that place does each share get? Third rung: the frame is cut to a two-digit dividend, and the child shares the tens before the ones. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: every written sum this year has started at the ones column, so the right hand end is where the pencil goes first.
wrong.move: starts with the ones, as in adding and taking away, and builds the quotient from the right.
wrong.screen: the working window is set on the ones as the child chose: six ones shared by three gives two, and four tens shared by three gives one ten with one ten left, and that ten has nowhere to go because the ones are already done. The frame then replays the division from the hundreds beside it, the two hundreds left over lit as they are changed into twenty tens and carried on, and both runs stay standing.

wrong.why: the zero feels like the end of the thousands, and nothing written down says the two thousands are still there.
wrong.move: writes a zero for the two thousands of two thousand seven hundred and thirty-six, then divides the seven hundreds on their own as if the two thousands had gone.
wrong.screen: the working window holds the two thousands with their place name and then does not move on alone: the two thousands are changed into twenty hundreds and slide right to join the seven, and the window reads twenty-seven hundreds. The child's seven hundreds stays written above it, and the check bar later rebuilds the child's answer as seven hundred and thirty-six, two thousand short of the dividend.

phases.screen: a frame with the dividend under its place headings and the working window on the biggest place
phases.soWhat: Long division starts with the digit in the biggest place, and what is left is carried on.

phases.win: the working window shows the new number with its place name and the next quotient digit settles
phases.does: fills the left slot, brings the next digit down, and divides the new number in the working window
phases.goal: each step brings down the next digit and divides everything that has built up
phases.says: Say what is left first. Now bring the next digit down. How many is that?
phases.check: Divide seven hundred and twenty-nine by three. Say what is left after each step, before you bring a digit down.
phases.feels: what is left is not finished with, it is the front half of the next number
phases.hands: Work nine hundred and fifty-three divided by four on the board, but stop after every step and ask the class to say what is left before anyone brings a digit down. Write each leftover in coloured chalk beside the next digit. Then rub one leftover out and ask where the next number came from.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is in the left slot? Second rung, the phase's: which digit comes down next, and what does it join? Third rung: the frame is cut to a two-digit dividend with one leftover, and the child fills the slot and brings down once. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the digit brought down is the one the eye is on, and the leftover is written further up the frame, away from it.
wrong.move: divides the five tens on their own and forgets the hundred that was left.
wrong.screen: the child's step is run in the working window as five tens shared by four, one ten each, while the hundred left from the first step stays lit in the left slot, still waiting. The window is then rebuilt with that hundred changed into ten tens and slid beside the five, and it reads fifteen tens; both working numbers stay written, one above the other.

wrong.why: a multiple that fits feels like the right one, and the strip was not climbed to the next rung to see.
wrong.move: takes two fours out of fifteen tens and carries seven tens on, when a third four still fits.
wrong.screen: the seven is written in the left slot as the child gave it and lit against the four at the bracket, seven beside four. The multiple strip lights the rung for three fours, twelve, which still fits under fifteen, and the rung for four fours, sixteen, which does not. The child's two stays beside the quotient cell and the step is offered again, nothing marked.

phases.screen: what is left after the first step, with the next digit waiting and the bring down arrow unlit
phases.soWhat: Each step brings down the next digit and divides everything that has built up.

phases.win: the zero lands above its place and the working number joins the next digit whole
phases.does: compares the working number with the divisor, writes the zero, and carries the whole number on
phases.goal: a zero goes in the quotient only when the number being divided is smaller than the divisor
phases.says: Is this number smaller than the divisor? Then how many fit?
phases.check: In eight hundred and seventeen divided by four, which step gets a zero? The last step leaves one over. Why does it get no zero?
phases.feels: a step with something left over can still fit the divisor several times, and only a number smaller than the divisor fits it none
phases.hands: Share seven hundreds, two tens and five ones among seven envelopes in play money. When only two tens are left to share among seven, ask what each envelope gets in tens, and write the zero. Then share the twenty-five ones. They leave four over, so ask whether that step gets a zero too, and why it does not.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the working number at this step, with its place name? Second rung, the phase's: is it smaller than the divisor? Third rung: the strip is laid against the working number rung by rung from times one, and the child says whether even the first rung fits. The zero key stays open, and the gate still reads it.

wrong.why: the summary box after the worked examples says a zero appears when a digit is not divisible by the divisor, and a step with something left over is exactly what that looks like. The test the first worked example states, smaller than the divisor, never comes into it.
wrong.move: writes a zero in the quotient at every step that leaves a remainder, because that step does not divide exactly.
wrong.screen: the gate hands back the zero offered for nine thousands and the one offered for thirty-six ones, and at each the strip lights the rungs that fit: one seven under nine, five sevens under thirty-six. Only at three tens does the whole strip stay dark, because three is smaller than seven, and there the gate opens and takes the grey zero. The child's zeros stay written beside the cells they were offered for, and the check bar rebuilds the four hundred they would make as two thousand eight hundred, beside the nine thousand eight hundred and thirty-six.

wrong.why: three tens gave nothing to write, and a step that gives nothing feels like a step with nothing to record.
wrong.move: leaves out a zero that belongs, writing one hundred and forty-five remainder one for nine thousand eight hundred and thirty-six divided by seven.
wrong.screen: the check bar multiplies seven by the child's one hundred and forty-five, adds the remainder, and the one thousand and sixteen it rebuilds slides under the dividend a whole place short. The frame is replayed with the gate over the tens cell, the strip stays dark against three tens because three is smaller than seven, the grey zero is taken, and the answer reads one thousand four hundred and five with every place filled.

phases.screen: a step whose working number is smaller than the divisor, with an earlier step that left a remainder still lit
phases.soWhat: A zero goes in the quotient only when the number being divided is smaller than the divisor. Whether the step divides exactly is not the test.
phases.concept: Smaller than the divisor means a zero

phases.win: the rebuilt number slides under the dividend and the two match digit for digit
phases.does: multiplies the divisor by the quotient, adds the remainder, and lays the result beside the dividend
phases.goal: divisor times quotient, add the remainder, gives back the dividend
phases.says: Multiply the divisor by your answer. Add what was left. Is it the number you started with?
phases.check: Someone says four thousand and nine divided by four is one thousand and two, remainder one. Check it by multiplying back.
phases.feels: the division is undone, and the dividend comes back only when the leftover is put back too
phases.hands: Give each pair a finished division on a card, some right and some with one step wrong. Each pair multiplies the divisor by the quotient, adds the remainder, and writes the result under the dividend. Ask which cards matched, and on the ones that did not, which step to look at first.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the divisor times the quotient? Second rung, the phase's: what was left at the end, and has it been added? Third rung: the check is cut to twenty-nine divided by four, and the child rebuilds twenty-nine from the answer. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the check is taught as the multiplication undoing the division, and the remainder is not part of any multiplication.
wrong.move: multiplies the divisor by the quotient and forgets to add the remainder.
wrong.screen: the check bar builds eight times six hundred and forty-seven, five thousand one hundred and seventy-six, and slides it under the dividend, where the ones do not match. The remainder is then lifted out of its slot and added on, the rebuilt number becomes five thousand one hundred and seventy-eight, and it matches digit for digit. Both rebuilt numbers stay drawn.

wrong.why: each subtraction in the working checks out on its own, and a step that was never written leaves no mark to look at.
wrong.move: accepts eighty-four remainder two for seven thousand five hundred and sixty-two divided by nine, because every step shown was right.
wrong.screen: the check bar builds nine times eighty-four, adds two, and the seven hundred and fifty-eight it makes slides under the dividend a whole place short. The frame is replayed step by step, and at the ones the two left is smaller than nine, so the gate takes the grey zero in the ones place. The check runs again on eight hundred and forty remainder two and matches digit for digit.

phases.screen: a finished division with the check bar empty under it
phases.soWhat: Divisor times quotient, add the remainder, gives back the dividend.

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the working number is smaller than the divisor. The gate lifts, the whole strip of multiples lights and then goes dark rung by rung from the top down, because not even the first rung fits, and the grey zero drops into the quotient cell at full size. Then the working number does not fall away: it slides right, whole, and the next digit comes down beside it, so three tens and six ones become thirty-six ones in front of the child. It can be replayed as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the frame holds the dividend under its place headings with the divisor behind the bracket, the quotient row empty, and the working window above the frame lit on the biggest place with its place name. On the second the first quotient digit already stands above its place and its multiple has been taken away, the left slot is empty, and the bring down arrow is drawn unlit beside the next digit. On the third the division has reached a step whose working number is smaller than the divisor, the gate is closed over that quotient cell, and an earlier step that left something over is still lit. On the fourth a finished division stands whole with the check bar empty under it. The running count at the top left holds the steps finished against the steps the division needs, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the biggest place heading, or the empty left slot, or the gate, or the empty check bar, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks which place goes first. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any dividend up to four digits and any divisor from two to nine, with the working window, the zero gate, the check bar and the blocks bay open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on starting with the biggest place, bringing down and dividing again, writing a zero only when the number is smaller than the divisor, and checking by multiplying back.
voiceLines: A number under its place headings, and a divisor at the door. Which place goes first?
Which place is the biggest? Share that one first.
Say what is left first. Now bring the next digit down. How many is that?
Is this number smaller than the divisor? Then how many fit?
Multiply the divisor by your answer. Add what was left. Is it the number you started with?
A new division. Name the biggest place before anything is shared.
Free play. Any dividend, any divisor from two to nine, with the gate and the check bar open.
Read the working window with its place name, then lay the multiples beside it.
Every step said, every zero where the number was smaller, and every check matched.

observations.why: Sharing the biggest things first leaves the smaller places free to take whatever is changed down into them.
observations.soWhat: Long division starts with the digit in the biggest place and carries what is left into the next place.
observations.observe: The first quotient digit landed above the biggest place, and what was left went on to the next place rather than away.

observations.why: What is left joins the next digit, so the next number to divide cannot be made without it.
observations.soWhat: Say what is left at every step, because it is the front half of the next number.
observations.observe: The bring down arrow would not light until the left slot held a number.

observations.why: A zero means no divisor fits at all, which happens only when the number is smaller than the divisor, and a step with something left over can still fit it several times.
observations.soWhat: The test for a zero is smaller than the divisor. A step that is not divisible but not smaller still gets a digit of one or more.
observations.observe: The gate took a zero at one step and handed it back at another step that left something over.

observations.why: Divisor times quotient counts every share handed out, and the remainder adds back what was never handed out.
observations.soWhat: Multiplying back and adding the remainder checks a division, and leaving the remainder off makes a right answer look wrong.
observations.observe: The rebuilt number slid under the dividend and matched it digit for digit.

model.frame: long division: place headings Th H T O, the quotient row above its places, the divisor at the left of the bracket, the dividend under it; each step's multiple is taken away and the next digit brought down
model.strip: the divisor times 1 to times 9, dragged (or tapped) onto the step in hand; a multiple bigger than the number does not fit
model.zeroGate: a lid over the quotient cell of the step in hand: the child taps it and types the digit on the pad; it takes a zero only when the number being divided is smaller than the divisor, and a digit only when that many fit
model.leftOver: under each multiple a cell waits: the child taps it and types what is left; it is taken only when the multiple plus it makes the number and it is smaller than the divisor, and the next digit cannot come down before it
model.checkCard: divisor times quotient, add the remainder, laid right-aligned over the dividend

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The frame is cleared and replayed from the biggest place heading: each step's multiple is taken away, what is left is changed into the next place as the next digit comes down, and it ends on the whole quotient and the remainder.

Phase 2: The frame is replayed step by step: what is left stays in the left over box, is changed into the next place, and joins the digit brought down, so the window reads the new number with its place; it ends on the quotient and the remainder (for the block of seats, each row's division fills its card and the total is added).

Phase 3: The frame is replayed; at a step whose number is smaller than the divisor the whole strip of multiples lights, goes dark rung by rung from the top, the lid lifts and a grey zero drops in at full size, and the number joins the next digit whole; it ends on the whole quotient and the remainder.

Phase 4: The check card builds divisor times quotient place by place (8 × 600, 8 × 640, 8 × 647), adds the remainder and lays the rebuilt number over the dividend, where it matches digit for digit; for the claimed 84 remainder 2 it first shows 758, a whole place short, then the missing zero is written in the ones and the check matches.

voice.opening: A number under its place headings, and a divisor at the door. Which place goes first?
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: Every step said, every zero where the number was smaller, and every check matched.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

items.planAnswer: Start with the 8 hundreds: 2 hundreds each, with 2 hundreds carried into the tens. The quotient is 282, remainder 0
684, remainder 0. The 2 thousands are smaller than 4, so the division starts with 27 hundreds

question.en: Divide 953 by 4, saying what is left at each step.

question.en: Divide 915 by 5, saying what is left after each step.

items.planQuestion: One block of a stand has three rows. Row A seats 738 divided by 6 people, row B seats 856 divided by 8, and row C seats 935 divided by 5. The block holds the three rows added together. How many people is that?

question.en: One block of a stand has three rows. Row A seats 738 ÷ 6 people. Row B seats 856 ÷ 8. Row C seats 935 ÷ 5. How many people sit in the block?

items.planAnswer: 417, because the rows seat 123, 107 and 187, and those add up to 417

items.planQuestion: 9836 is divided by 7. At which step does a zero go in the quotient, and why? What is the answer?

question.en: Divide 9,836 by 7. Look for the step where the number is smaller than 7.

items.planAnswer: At the tens: 3 tens is smaller than 7, so a zero goes in the tens place. The answer is 1405 remainder 1

items.planQuestion: In 612 divided by 6, what goes in the tens place of the quotient, and why?

question.en: In 612 divided by 6, what goes in the tens place of the quotient?

items.planAnswer: A zero, because 1 ten is smaller than 6; the quotient is 102
The quotient is 1005, remainder 5: a zero goes in the hundreds and a zero in the tens, because 0 hundreds and then 4 tens are each smaller than 8

items.planQuestion: Divide 5178 by 8, and check the answer by multiplying back.

question.en: 5,178 divided by 8 is 647 remainder 2. Check it by multiplying back: what is 8 times 647?

items.planAnswer: 647 remainder 2, and 8 times 647 is 5176, add 2 makes 5178

items.planQuestion: Check by multiplying back whether 3097 divided by 6 is 516 remainder 1.

question.en: Is 3,097 divided by 6 equal to 516 remainder 1? Check it. First, what is 6 times 516?

items.planAnswer: Yes: 6 times 516 is 3096, and adding 1 gives 3097

items.planQuestion: A child says 7562 divided by 9 is 84 remainder 2. Multiply back to test it, then find the right answer.

question.en: A child says 7,562 divided by 9 is 84 remainder 2. Multiply back to test it, then find the right answer.

items.planAnswer: 9 times 84 is 756, add 2 makes 758, not 7562, so it is wrong. The quotient is 840 remainder 2: the last 2 ones are smaller than 9, so a zero goes in the ones place

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page; finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }

phases.concept: Smaller than the divisor means a zero

getState: toolId, mediaId, mode, mountPhase, phase, phases, conceptId, objectiveIds, step, steps, item, items, stage (teach, demo, ask, win, idle, summary, free), question, questionText, choices, typed, keypadOpen, tries, answered, firstTry, score, maxScore, answerShown (only after the answer), complete, questionCount, muted, speaking, voice, mascot, summaryRow, played, dividend, divisor, frameStep, working, null, quotientDigits, x, leftAtStep, zeroOffered, padToCell, kind, checked

terminalEvent.name: finished
terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

sounds: Web Audio, no files: correct, wrong (soft), win, and a tick when a piece snaps

voiceLines.en: A number under its place headings, and a divisor at the door. Which place goes first?
Which place is the biggest? Share that one first.
Say what is left first. Now bring the next digit down. How many is that?
Is this number smaller than the divisor? Then how many fit?
Multiply the divisor by your answer. Add what was left. Is it the number you started with?
A new division. Name the biggest place before anything is shared.
Free play. Any dividend, any divisor from two to nine, with the gate and the check bar open.
Read the working window with its place name, then lay the multiples beside it.
Every step said, every zero where the number was smaller, and every check matched.
